'''''Kalanchoe pinnata''''', commonly known as '''cathedral bells''', '''air plant''', '''life plant''', '''miracle leaf''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date = 29 June 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Sad |first1=Sadman |title=Goethe plant: A Unique Medicinal Plant |url=https://thegreenpagebd.com/goethe-plant/ |website=The Green Page |access-date=16 November 2023 |date=12 September 2020}}</ref> and '''love bush''',<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Acevedo Rodríguez |first1=Pedro |last2=Rojas-Sandoval |first2=Julissa |title=Kalanchoe pinnata (cathedral bells) |url=https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/10.1079/cabicompendium.29328 |website=CABI Digital Library |date=2022 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.29328 |access-date=3 December 2023|doi-access=free }}</ref> is a [[succulent plant]] native to [[Madagascar]]. It is a popular [[houseplant]] and has become naturalized in tropical and subtropical areas. The species is distinctive for the profusion of miniature plantlets that form on the margins of its leaves, a trait it has in common with some other members of ''[[Bryophyllum]]'' (now included in ''[[Kalanchoe]]'').<ref name="POWO">{{Cite web|title=''Kalanchoe pinnata'' (Lam.) Pers.|url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:274438-1|access-date=2020-10-14|website=Plants of the World Online|publisher=Kew Science}}</ref>

==Description==
The leaves of this species are thick, fleshy, elliptical in shape, curved, with a [[crenate]] or serrated margin, often reddish. Simple at the base of the stem, the leaves are imparipinnate at the top, {{convert|10-30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long, with three to five pairs of fleshy limb lobes.

The leaves are remarkable for their ability to produce [[bulbil]]s. At their margin, between the teeth, adventitious buds appear, which produce roots, stems and leaves. This is a fairly common trait in the section ''Bryophyllum''. The fruits are [[Follicle (fruit)|follicles]] (10–15 mm) which are found in the persistent calyx and corolla.<ref>Kamboj Anjoo, Ajay Kumar Saluja,"  Microscopical and Preliminary Phytochemical Studies on Aerial Part (Leaves and Stem) of Bryophyllum pinnatum Kurz." PHCOG J., Vol. 2, n° 9, 2010, p. 254–9</ref>

The terminal [[inflorescence]] is a [[panicle]], with many pendent, red-orange flowers. The [[calyx (botany)|calyx]] is formed of a long tube, red at the base, veined with yellowish green (or green spotted with reddish brown), with four very small triangular lobes at the end. The tubular [[corolla (botany)|corolla]], with a pronounced constriction separating the subspherical part of the [[ovoid]] part, is terminated by four lobes which reaches {{convert|5|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} in length. It is yellowish in color with red-purple streaks. The eight stamens, each about {{convert|4|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} long, are in two whorls, welded on the corolla. The ovary has four [[carpel]]s, slightly fused together in the center, with slender styles.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | doi = 10.5586/asbp.1996.022
| title = Morphogenesis of propagules in viviparous species ''Bryophyllum daigremontianum'' and ''B. calycinum''
| journal = Acta Societatis Botanicorum Poloniae
| volume = 65
| pages = 127–133
| year = 1996

| last2 = Bragina | first2 = E. A.
| last3 = Titova | first3 = G. E.
| issue = 1–2

}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Kalanchoe pinnata'' is native to [[Madagascar]].<ref name=GRIN/> and has become naturalized in tropical and subtropical areas, inhabiting warm and [[temperate climate]]s from [[sea level]] to {{convert|2600|m|ft|-2|abbr=on}}, occupying sites on rock in tropical evergreen and [[Madagascar dry deciduous forests|dry deciduous forests]], as well as [[Madagascar subhumid forests|montane forests]]. It is found in parts of Asia, Africa, Australia, New Zealand, the [[West Indies]], Bermuda, [[Macaronesia]], the [[Mascarenes]], [[Brazil]], [[Suriname]], the [[Galapagos]] Islands, [[Melanesia]], [[Polynesia]], and [[Hawaii]].<ref name="POWO" /><ref>{{GRIN | ''Kalanchoe pinnata'' | 21076 | access-date = 2007-10-01}}</ref>
In many of these, such as [[Hawaii]], it is regarded as an [[invasive species]].<ref>{{cite web
 |title       = ''Kalanchoe pinnata''
 |work        = Hawaii's Most Invasive Horticultural Plants
 |url         = http://www.state.hi.us/dlnr/dofaw/hortweeds/species/kalpin.htm
 |access-date  = 2007-10-01
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20071103170324/http://www.state.hi.us/dlnr/dofaw/hortweeds/species/kalpin.htm
 |archive-date = 2007-11-03
}}</ref>
Much of the reason for the widespread naturalization of this plant can be traced to its popularity as a garden plant.

==Taxonomy and nomenclature==
The plant ''Kalanchoe pinnata'' was harvested by [[Pierre Sonnerat]] in [[Isle de France (Mauritius)|Isle de France]] ([[Mauritius]]) and communicated to Lamarck who described it in 1786 as the ''Cotyledon pinnata''. Subsequently, the Paris naturalist [[Christiaan Hendrik Persoon]] reclassified it in the Kalanchoe (calling it ''Calanchoe pinnata 1805-1807'', with an orthographic variant). It was first published in Syn. Pl. vol.1 on page 446 in 1805.<ref name="POWO" />
At the same time, in [[London]], the botanist [[Richard Anthony Salisbury]] described the same plant from a specimen received from [[Bengal]], under the name of ''Bryophyllum calycinum'',<ref>''Bryophyllum calycinum'' Salisb. in Parad. Lond. 1: t. 3 (1805)</ref> and at the same time created the new genus ''Bryophyllum''.<ref>V. Hequet Mr Le Corre, F. Rigault V. Blanfort "  Invasive alien species of New Caledonia  ", Southern Province Convention, vol.  C153-08, 2009</ref>

The specific Latin [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] "pinnata" is the feminine form of the Latin adjective ''pinnatus'', meaning "[[pinnate]]".<ref>Leslie Taylor, The Healing Power of Rainforest Herbs: A Guide to Understanding and Using Herbal Medicinals, Square One Publishers, 2004, 268  p.</ref>

It has several local names in its native Madagascar: ''falatanantsifaona'', ''malainana'', ''rendadiaka'', ''sodifafana'' and ''tsilafafa''.<ref name=MDME>{{Cite dictionary|url=https://en.mondemalgache.org/bins/taxonLists?kingdom=B&order=1&range=K#Kalanchoepinnata|title=Botanical scientific names|dictionary=Malagasy Dictionary and Malagasy Encyclopedia|language=en|date=2001|editor-first=Jean-Marie|editor-last=de La Beaujardière|access-date=2022-11-02|archive-date=2022-11-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221102001710/https://en.mondemalgache.org/bins/taxonLists?kingdom=B&order=1&range=K#Kalanchoepinnata|url-status=dead}}</ref> In the Philippines, it is known as {{lang|fil|katakataka}} or {{lang|fil|kataka-taka}} which is an adjective meaning 'astonishing' or 'remarkable'.<ref>{{cite web| title = Katakataka | work = Philippine Medicinal Plants| url =http://www.stuartxchange.com/Katakataka.html| access-date = 2008-11-20}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=''Kataka-taka''|work=Filipino Herbs Healing Wonders|url=http://www.filipinoherbshealingwonders.filipinovegetarianrecipe.com/herbs_pics/katakataka.php|access-date=2008-11-20|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081017204349/http://www.filipinoherbshealingwonders.filipinovegetarianrecipe.com/herbs_pics/katakataka.php|archive-date=October 17, 2008 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web| title = ''Katakataka'' It usually used as a medicine to cure kidney stone.| work = Tagalog English Dictionary| url = http://www.bansa.org/dictionaries/tgl/?type=search&data=katakataka| access-date = 2008-11-20| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120218215902/http://www.bansa.org/dictionaries/tgl/?type=search&data=katakataka| archive-date = 2012-02-18| url-status = dead}}</ref>

The writer [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe]] (1749–1832), who was an amateur [[Natural history|naturalist]] of some repute, was "passionately fond" of this plant and liked to give baby plantlets of the air plant, as gifts to friends who visited his home. He also discussed his air plant at length in an essay in 1817, titled in {{Langx|de|Geschichte meiner botanischen Studien}} ("History of my botanical studies").<ref>{{cite web |title=Johann Wolfgang von Goethe als Gartenfreund - der Botaniker und seine Studien |url=https://www.garten-literatur.de/Leselaube/goethe/goethe2_botanik.htm |website=www.garten-literatur.de |access-date=16 November 2023 |language=German}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
In temperate regions, ''Kalanchoe pinnata'' is grown as an indoor [[ornamental plant]]. Like most succulents, it cannot survive hard frost and will not thrive in environments in which the temperature drops below {{convert|10|C|F}}. It favours well-drained soil, the roots being otherwise susceptible to rot. In the tropics, ''K. pinnata'' is grown outdoors in gardens, from which it may escape to become naturalised - often as an invasive weed.

==Toxicity and traditional medicine==
In common with other species belonging to the Crassulaceae (including certain members of the genera ''[[Tylecodon]]'', [[Cotyledon (genus)|''Cotyledon'']] and ''[[Adromischus]]''), ''Kalanchoe pinnata'' has been found to contain [[bufadienolide]] [[cardiac glycosides]]<ref>{{cite journal
  | last = Steyn
  | first = Pieter S
  | author2=van Heerden, Fanie R.
  | title = Bufadienolides of plant and animal origin
  | publisher = Royal Society of Chemistry
  | journal = Natural Product Reports
  | year = 1998
  | volume = 15
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 397–413
 | doi = 10.1039/a815397y
 | pmid = 9736996
 | s2cid = 30031690
 | url = http://www.rsc.org/delivery/_ArticleLinking/DisplayArticleForFree.cfm?doi=a815397y
  | access-date = 2007-09-19| url-access = subscription
  }}
</ref> These can cause cardiac [[poison]]ing, particularly in grazing animals.<ref name="pmid3778371">{{cite journal |title=Hearts and flowers: ''Bryophyllum'' poisoning of cattle |journal=Aust. Vet. J. |volume=63 |issue=7 |pages=222–7 |date=July 1986 |pmid=3778371 |doi= 10.1111/j.1751-0813.1986.tb03000.x|author1=McKenzie RA |author2=Dunster PJ }}</ref><ref name="pmid3439945">{{cite journal |title=The toxicity to cattle and bufadienolide content of six ''Bryophyllum'' species |journal=Aust. Vet. J. |volume=64 |issue=10 |pages=298–301 |date=October 1987 |pmid=3439945 |doi= 10.1111/j.1751-0813.1987.tb07330.x|author1=McKenzie RA |author2=Franke FP |author3=Dunster PJ }}</ref>

''Bryophyllum pinnatum'' has been recorded in Trinidad and Tobago as being used as a traditional treatment for [[hypertension]].<ref name="pmid17040567">{{cite journal |author=Lans CA |title=Ethnomedicines used in Trinidad and Tobago for urinary problems and diabetes mellitus |journal=J Ethnobiol Ethnomed |volume=2 |pages=45 |year=2006 |pmid=17040567 |pmc=1624823 |doi=10.1186/1746-4269-2-45 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In traditional medicine, the juice of the leaves is also used for kidney stones; although there is ongoing research into and some scientific evidence for this use, further research is required. In the [[French Antilles]], ''Kalanchoe pinnata'' called locally as ''zeb maltet'', is used in local application against [[headaches]]. For the people of the Amazon, Kalanchoe has multiple uses: the Creoles use it roasted against inflammations and [[cancer]] and as an infusion, and as a popular remedy for [[fever]]s. The [[Palikur]] people of [[Brazil]] and [[French Guiana]] apply a preparation of the juice of Kalanchoe leaves mixed with coconut oil to their foreheads to treat headache.<ref>Hermann Jacobsen : The Succulent Encyclopedia . 3. Edition. Fischer, Jena 1983, p. 275.</ref>

===Chemical constituents===
[[Bufadienolide]] compounds isolated from ''Bryophyllum pinnatum'' include [[bryophillin A]],  [[bersaldegenin-3-acetate]], and [[bryophillin C]].<ref name="SUPRATMAN FUJITA AKIYAMA HAYASHI 2001 pp. 947–949">{{cite journal |last1=SUPRATMAN |first1=Unang |last2=FUJITA |first2=Tomoyuki |last3=AKIYAMA |first3=Kohki |last4=HAYASHI |first4=Hideo |last5=MURAKAMI |first5=Akira |last6=SAKAI |first6=Hirofumi |last7=KOSHIMIZU |first7=Koichi |last8=OHIGASHI |first8=Hajime |year=2001 |title=Anti-tumor Promoting Activity of Bufadienolides from Kalanchoe pinnata and K. daigremontiana × butiflora |journal=Bioscience, Biotechnology, and Biochemistry |publisher=Oxford University Press (OUP) |volume=65 |issue=4 |pages=947–949 |doi=10.1271/bbb.65.947 |issn=0916-8451 |pmid=11388478|doi-access=free }}</ref> Bryophillin C also showed insecticidal properties.<ref name="SUPRATMAN FUJITA AKIYAMA HAYASHI 2000 pp. 1310–1312">{{cite journal |last1=SUPRATMAN |first1=Unang |last2=FUJITA |first2=Tomoyuki |last3=AKIYAMA |first3=Kohki |last4=HAYASHI |first4=Hideo |year=2000 |title=New Insecticidal Bufadienolide, Bryophyllin C, from''Kalanchoe pinnata'' |journal=Bioscience, Biotechnology, and Biochemistry |publisher=Informa UK Limited |volume=64 |issue=6 |pages=1310–1312 |doi=10.1271/bbb.64.1310 |issn=0916-8451 |pmid=10923811|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Phytochemical studies of ''Kalanchoe pinnata'' have identified the presence of [[triterpene]]s, [[steroid]], [[phenanthrene]], [[flavonoid]], [[flavones]], [[chalcone]]s, [[taraxasterol]], [[aurone]]s, [[phenolic acid]], [[caffeic acid]], [[syringic acid]], [[Malic acid|malic]], [[Oxalic acid|oxalic]] and [[ferulic]] acid. [[Bufadienolide]]s and [[phenanthrene]] are toxic compounds. Two [[Calf (animal)|calves]] fed for 48 hours with K. pinnata have been reported to have died due to [[ataxia]] and severe [[cardiac arrhythmia]].<ref>Bernard Descoings: ''Kalanchoe pinnata'' . In: Urs Eggli (ed.): Succulent lexicon. Crassulaceae (thick-leaved plants) . Eugen Ulmer, Stuttgart 2003, {{ISBN|3-8001-3998-7}}, p  175</ref>

Balakrishnan|author3= Paresh V. Churi|author4= S. Kalesh|author5= Satya Prakash|author6= Krushnamegh Kunte|url=http://threatenedtaxa.org/index.php/JoTT/article/view/3104/4402|journal=Journal of Threatened Taxa|volume=10|quote=260. ''Bryophyllum pinnatum'' (Lam.) Oken: Talicada nyseus nyseus (Lycaenidae)|issue=4|pages=11495–11550|via=JoTT|doi=10.11609/jott.3104.10.4.11495-11550|doi-access=free}}</ref>
